questions.q: What is the master database responsible for?
options: Recording all system-level information for the instance, including the existence of every other database
Storing only user-created tables
Holding backup files
Nothing — it's an empty placeholder database
questions.explain: master is the instance's own bookkeeping database — logins, configuration, and the list of every database on the server.

questions.q: What is the model database used for?
options: It's the template SQL Server copies whenever a new database is created
It stores SQL Server Agent job schedules
It's a workspace for temporary tables
It's only used during installation and never again
questions.explain: Any setting changed in model is inherited by every database created afterward.

questions.q: Where do local #temp tables and table variables physically live?
options: tempdb
master
msdb
model
questions.explain: tempdb is the workspace for temporary objects and intermediate result sets, tying directly back to Lesson 93.

options: SQL Server Agent — scheduling jobs, alerts, and tracking backup history
Storing every user table in the instance
Holding the template for new databases
Encrypting all databases on the instance
questions.explain: msdb is the home for SQL Server Agent's scheduled jobs, alerts, and backup/restore history.

questions.q: Why shouldn't you directly INSERT or UPDATE rows in master or msdb?
options: It can corrupt the instance's own bookkeeping — proper DDL (CREATE DATABASE, CREATE LOGIN) and administrative tools exist specifically to avoid this
SQL Server physically blocks all writes to those databases with no exceptions
It's allowed and actually recommended for advanced users
Those databases are read-only by default and cannot be written to at all
questions.explain: SQL Server provides safe, structured ways (DDL, SSMS, SQL-SMO) to manage system-level changes instead of manual edits.
